newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan falls hook, line and sinker for fishing.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan falls hook, line and sinker for fishing.

text.p: These are not good times for Japanese fish.
Not only is there a huge increase in anglers personally trying to turn them into sushi, but even their last bite is no longer likely to be live bait but inedible lures and flies.
It all adds up to the latest craze to sweep trend-conscious Japan.
Fishing is cool, fashionable and good for the soul.

In the past year, a government report estimated the number of anglers had grown by about one million and the private Nomura Research Institute forecasts the current market for fly and lure fishing will almost double to nearly $1 billion by 1999.
The craze crosses all age and class lines with a host of new television shows on fishing a testimony to how the nation has fallen hook, line and sinker for the pastime.
Japan already leads the world in fish consumption with its 123 million population eating about 10 times more fish than the United States.
But the love affair with fish has entered new waters with a record 19 million Japanese a year now casting their own bait, flies and lures.
The government report on leisure estimated anglers spent an average $180 a year on equipment, cast their lines about 11 times a year, and paid on average $38 for each session.

With such a vast profitable market comes, as usual in Japan, government guidance in the form of the Japanese Sports Fishing Association (JSFA), an advisory and regulatory body devoted to keeping Japan a land of clean and teeming waters, as well as teaching schoolchildren how to respectfully approach fishing.

The craze has led to the removal of many "No Fishing" signs around lakes and streams as local authorities issue permits and licences, using the money raised to replenish fish stocks in rivers and lakes.
"The ones in the sea can take care of themselves," says Kiyoji Hattori, the JSFA senior director.
The more the demand for fishing, the more the fees roll in, the more money spent on stocking fishing spots.
"The more the merrier. We're imposing no limits as yet," Hattori said.
Once nearly-deserted, river banks, jetties and lake shores now teem with shoulder-to-shoulder anglers, all breathing stress-free air, and enjoying their view of nature.

"Fishing's a tonic for me," beamed one Saturday angler in a downtown Tokyo park. "I don't catch much here and those I do I put in the keep net, weigh when I've finished and then let them go back. I just like to meditate in nature and fishing's a good excuse for doing it."

"The thought of putting hooks into maggots and worms never appealed to me," says Mariko Hara, an office worker. "But fly fishing is wonderful. I usually ask my boyfriend to take the hook out of the fish's mouth."
Black bass in particular is the current hot fish and manufacturers cannot keep up with the demand for lures from a new young generation who like to go fishing with "clean hands".
Magazines and television programmes have stoked the promotion of fishing to young people looking for the in-thing in the "Great Outdoors".
And according to the Japan Fishing Tackle Manufacturers Association, the popularity of fishing can only keep growing far into the future as a "family sport".

Jammed-packed closets in the small homes where most Japanese live, are being cleared out of equipment used for the country's past obsessions with sports like tennis, golf and skiing to make way for fishing tackle.
China and South Korea are reaping an export boom by providing most of the inexpensive equipment needed by the everyday angler.
The top end of the market is supplied by Sweden and the United States while Japanese manufacturers are starting to apply their own high craftsmanship to the fishing craft.

To cope with Japan's latest sporting fad, which far exceeds past golf, tennis and skiing participation, major manufacturers like Daiwa Seiko Inc are selling beginner fishing kits at $200 complete with instructional videos.
A company spokesman said fishing's popularity with young television personalities had created a new generation of anglers far removed from the stuffy, middle-aged image of the past.
Japan's current economic problems, which have resulted in higher unemployment, earlier retirement and shorter working hours, is also responsible for many of the new anglers.

One ex-bank employee explained: "After 30 years of being away from home most of the day and evening, my wife now finds it difficult to cope with me being around the house all the time. So I get out as often as I can, cast my line and sit there enjoying my new freedom and a few cans of beer."
You can even do your fishing in your lunch hour.
In downtown Tokyo, it's not unusual to see office workers spending their lunch hour munching sandwiches while dangling their lines in an artificial trout pool.
